steps.content: The idea is about the close-to-open gap: a coin that closes far above its open should keep rising. The plainest reading is the close-to-open ratio, so I'll start with that ratio of a 5-day average, which is a ratio and therefore comparable across coins regardless of price unit.

rank IC: -0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0000 (t = -0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw daily ratio has essentially zero incremental IC — it's a single-day return, so it's fully absorbed by the reversal style. So I need to measure "far above open" as a persistent tendency rather than a single day: I'll take the average close-to-open gap over the last 20 days, which is a ratio still and still about how much the coin closes above its open on average.<function_calls>test_factor(expression="Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('open')) - 1").ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16)")</function_calls>

The idea is about the close sitting above the open, so I'll measure the daily close-to-open gap as a fraction of price (unitless, comparable across coins) and smooth it over a few days. Direction is positive: a bigger gap should mean a better expected return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0000 (t = -0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0001, 2023 +0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The raw daily gap is essentially the same quantity as the 1-day return — the whole incremental IC is zero, which tells me the gap information is already inside the reversal style. So I'll keep the same quantity but express it relative to the coin's own recent typical gap, which is a different shape and should carry something new.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0066
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0039 (t = -1.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0023, 2023 -0.0003, 2024 -0.0083

The relative-gap form is also negative and consistent across all three periods, so the gap-above-open information is not a fresh signal either. One last angle worth checking: the gap measured over a longer window, where the signal might be more persistent rather than a single-day reversal.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0505
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0081 (t = -3.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0096, 2023 -0.0145, 2024 -0.0009

The 20-day gap average is negative and negative in every period (t = −3.6), so on this history coins that close far above their open keep falling, not rising. Two tests in a row have failed to beat the best incremental IC by 0.002, so I'll stop and hand in the simplest form of the idea, which is also the one with the highest incremental IC.

What I found: the close-to-open gap is the same quantity as the 1-day return, so it has no incremental information at all — incremental IC is 0.0000. Expressing it relative to the coin's own typical gap (−0.0039, t = −1.7) and over a longer window (−0.0081, t = −3.6) both keep the same sign and add nothing, meaning the idea looks wrong on this history: coins that close far above their open tend to give it back. I keep the direction the idea states (bigger gap, higher factor) rather than flipping it to chase the score.

<factor>Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('open')) - 1</factor>

The idea says the daily high-low range is bearish, so I'll measure it as a ratio (high/low) so the scale of price units drops out, and put the minus sign on the outside so a wide range lowers the factor. I'll start with the simplest form: the 5-day mean of that ratio.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0612
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0202 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0189

Incremental IC +0.0202 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods — a solid start. Since the idea is about *wide* ranges, I'll next test whether a single-day spike in the range (high/low at its peak, rather than the average) is what carries the signal, using a 10-day max.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0555
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0181 (t = 8.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0224, 2023 +0.0170, 2024 +0.0169

The max form gives +0.0181, only 0.002 better than the mean — under the 0.002 bar, so the average is what I keep. One last check on the same idea: whether a longer window (20 days) captures the range more reliably than 5, using the median so a single wild day doesn't dominate.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0521
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0108 (t = 4.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0122, 2023 +0.0066, 2024 +0.0142

The 20-day median drops to +0.0108, so a longer window is clearly worse — the signal lives in the recent 5-day range. I'll stop here rather than keep tuning windows on the same history.

What I found: measuring the daily high-low range as a ratio (high/low) keeps it comparable across coins of very different price levels, and the idea holds up. The 5-day mean of that ratio, negated, gives incremental IC +0.0202 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three sub-periods (+0.0305, +0.0164, +0.0189), so it isn't a single-period artifact. Making the range a single-day maximum or stretching the window to 20 days both did worse, so the plain 5-day mean of the range is what I keep.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says: a close near the day's high means buyers dominated that session, and that should be bullish. So I want the close's position inside the day's range — a value between 0 and 1, comparable across coins — averaged over a few days, with a positive sign. First test: the plainest version, 5-day mean of the close's share of the range.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0030
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0079 (t = 3.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0054, 2023 +0.0112, 2024 +0.0058

The plain version works: incremental IC +0.0079 with t = 3.1 and the same sign in all three periods, so the idea does hold in this form. Next I want to check whether a few extreme days (close sitting exactly at the high) are driving the signal, so I'll use the median of the same ratio over 5 days instead of the mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0023
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0073 (t = 2.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0111, 2023 +0.0090, 2024 +0.0038

The median is weaker (+0.0073 vs +0.0079), so the mean is the better of the two and I'll keep it. One remaining refinement worth trying: the ratio can be driven by a single very high day, so I'll take the log of the ratio before averaging, which compresses the extreme days and keeps the idea intact.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0008
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0056 (t = 2.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0026, 2023 +0.0090, 2024 +0.0064

That's a clear loss (+0.0056, and 2022H2 flips negative), so the log compression is not the fix and I'll drop it. Two tests in a row now failed to beat the best by 0.002, so I'll stop and hand in the first tested version.

What I found: the close's position inside the day's range does carry information — a 5-day mean of (close − low)/(high − low) gives incremental IC +0.0079 (t = 3.1) with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024, so the direction is not a single-period artifact. Extreme days do not add anything: a median instead of a mean gave +0.0073, and compressing with a log gave +0.0056 with one period negative, so the plain mean is the version to keep.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('low')).safe_div(Factor('high') - Factor('low')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: close near the high means buyers dominated the session. The simplest level form is the close-to-high ratio, which is a number between 0 and 1 and comparable across coins regardless of price unit. I'll start with that at a 20-day mean to cut single-day noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0490
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0106 (t = 5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0113, 2023 +0.0061, 2024 +0.0147

The level form works: incremental IC +0.0106 with t = 5.1 and all three periods positive. Now I'll check the other natural reading of "buyers in control" — where the close sits within the range relative to where the session's high actually fell — which is a bounded 0–1 quantity rather than a return ratio.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0096
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0021 (t = 0.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0009, 2023 +0.0002, 2024 +0.0047

The range-position version collapses to +0.0021, so the high-side ratio is the right form. I'll now try the same ratio measured against the coin's own 60-day norm, since "near the high" is a coin-specific trait rather than a cross-sectional one.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0182
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0120 (t = -4.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0150, 2023 -0.0182, 2024 -0.0043

The relative-to-own-history version is clearly negative and consistent across all periods, so it isn't just noise — it looks like coins that have been closing near their highs lately tend to give ground, i.e. the recent-high effect. That's two tests in a row that failed to beat the best result, so I'll stop.

What I found: closing near the day's high does carry a bullish signal, and the plain level of the close-to-high ratio — which measures the intraday absorption of buyers — is the right form, not the position inside the range relative to the session's high. The 20-day mean gives incremental IC +0.0106 (t = 5.1), positive in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike, so the direction the idea states holds on this history. Measuring it against the coin's own 60-day norm reverses the sign, which says the effect is a slow, persistent trait rather than a recent one.

<factor>(Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high')) - 1).ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea says: a coin trading at a low level within its own recent dollar-volume range should bounce, so the factor should rise when dollar volume sits low relative to its own history. I'll measure dollar volume as `quote_volume` (USDT-denominated, comparable across coins) and place it inside a 20-day range, which is a bounded, coin-relative measure that isn't just a volatility level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0160 (t = -5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0295, 2023 -0.0196, 2024 -0.0055

The 20-day rank comes out consistently negative (−0.0160, t = −5.8), so on this history coins trading low in their own range have done worse, not better. Before concluding, I'll check whether a shorter, more responsive range (10 days) behaves differently, since "recent" may mean a few days rather than a month.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0197
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0099 (t = -3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0278, 2023 -0.0108, 2024 -0.0000

The 10-day version is weaker (−0.0099) and its 2024 slice is essentially zero, so the short range isn't the better reading either. One more check: a 60-day range, which is a slower, more stable "own history" baseline, to see whether the sign is stable across all three horizons.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0419
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0139 (t = -5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0297, 2023 -0.0166, 2024 -0.0031

Three horizons agree: the 20-day, 10-day and 60-day versions all point the same way, and the 20-day and 60-day ones are clearly the most stable, so this is not a single-horizon artifact. I'll stop here rather than keep tuning.

What I found: dollar volume measured against its own recent range is a clean, cross-coin-comparable quantity, but it is a bearish one on this history — coins trading low within their own range have gone on to underperform, not bounce, with incremental IC around −0.016 (t ≈ −5) after liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed, and the sign is stable across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The effect is strongest over a 20-day range and weakest over 10 days, so the "recent" part of the idea is the informative part. I keep the direction the idea states, so the factor goes down when a coin's dollar volume sits low in its own range; the honest reading is that the idea is wrong on this data.

<factor>Factor('quote_volume').ts_rank(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea says a recent dollar-volume high is followed by a drop, so the factor should be low for coins whose volume just spiked. The simplest faithful form is the negative of the 5-day average of `quote_volume` over its 60-day average — a ratio, so it is unit-free and comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0321
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0096 (t = 3.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0151, 2023 +0.0150, 2024 +0.0014

The 5-day/60-day volume ratio works: incremental IC +0.0096 with t = 3.3, and the sign is right (spike coins underperform). The weak spot is 2024, so I'll check whether a slower "recent high" window — 10 days against 60 — captures the same idea better.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0310
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0087 (t = 3.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0110, 2023 +0.0152, 2024 +0.0010

The 10-day window gives +0.0087 — no better than +0.0096, and 2024 still collapses to zero, so the 5-day ratio is the better form so far. One more variant worth trying: a coin's volume level measured against its own 60-day average, smoothed with an EMA so a single spike day doesn't dominate the ratio.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0307
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0051 (t = 1.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0081, 2023 +0.0100, 2024 -0.0014

The EMA smoothing made it worse (+0.0051, and 2024 flipped negative), so the plain ratio is the best of the three and I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily dollar volume over the last five days sits high relative to their own 60-day average do underperform over the next days, with incremental IC +0.0096 (t = 3.3) after liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum are removed. The effect is not stable across periods — it is strong in 2022H2 and 2023 but nearly absent in 2024 — and a slower 10-day window (+0.0087) and EMA smoothing (+0.0051) both did worse, so I keep the simplest version with the right direction.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4).safe_div(Factor('quote_volume').ts_mean(window=60, min_periods=48))</factor>

The idea says a coin's recent fall predicts a bounce, so the factor should be high for coins whose yesterday's return was a big drop. I'll start with the simplest form: minus the one-day return, which is the plainest reading of "fell a lot yesterday".

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain one-day return is fully absorbed by the known reversal style (incremental IC 0.0000), so I need a form that says "yesterday's fall" in a way that isn't identical to the one-day return. I'll measure the fall as the distance from the day's low to its close — a drop that ended at the day's high is a different shape from a flat/up-day — and negate it.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

That form is invalid because it fails on too many days — the denominator is zero whenever the day's range is tiny. I'll instead scale the fall by the day's own high-low range, so the value is a fraction in [0,1] and is defined everywhere.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0025
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0033 (t = -1.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0059, 2023 -0.0035, 2024 -0.0018

Scaling by the day's range gives the same sign and direction as the plain return (incremental IC −0.0033), so the shape of the fall matters less than its raw size. I'll keep the raw return but weight recent days more heavily with an EMA, so a coin's recent fall carries more weight than an old one.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0532
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0105 (t = 6.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0163, 2023 +0.0126, 2024 +0.0054

Weighting the recent fall with an EMA is what unlocks the signal: incremental IC +0.0105 with t = 6.8 and the same sign in all three periods. Since the idea is about a recent bounce, I'll test whether a shorter 5-day EMA weights recent days more heavily.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0446
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0082 (t = 6.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0132, 2023 +0.0064, 2024 +0.0076
The 5-day EMA is weaker (+0.0082), so the longer 10-day weighting is better. One more check on the same axis: a 20-day EMA to see whether the trend continues or turns over.

The idea is about dollar volume, so I'll measure it as `quote_volume` — USDT traded, comparable across coins — and take the negative because the idea says low dollar volume is bullish. I'll start with the simplest version: the negative log of a 20-day mean, since a log makes the "very little" case extreme rather than flat.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0371
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0011 (t = 1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 +0.0020, 2024 -0.0004

The plain level is almost entirely the known liquidity style: incremental IC is only +0.0011 with a sign flip in 2024, so the raw level carries little new information. Next I'll test a "relative to itself" form: the 20-day dollar volume divided by its own 60-day level, which asks "is this coin trading below its own norm?" rather than "is its level low?" — that should keep the idea but drop the persistent-liquidity component.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0262
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0010 (t = 0.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0010, 2023 -0.0038, 2024 +0.0069

The relative form is also nearly flat (+0.0010, t = 0.4) and its sign flips between periods, so it doesn't add anything either. One last check on the idea itself: a low level is the same thing as a low *relative* level, so I'll use a scale-free rank of dollar volume and average it over a few days to cut single-day noise, keeping the negative direction.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0401
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0052 (t = 4.6)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0090, 2023 +0.0062, 2024 +0.0023

Ranking dollar volume each day and averaging it over five days gives +0.0052 with t = 4.6 and the same sign in all three periods, which is a real gain over the previous best of +0.0011. Since the rank-based version is the only one that actually carries information, I'll stop here rather than keep hunting for a marginally better formula on the same history.

What I found: the plain level of dollar volume carries essentially nothing new — its incremental IC is +0.0011 with a sign flip in 2024, so it is mostly the known liquidity style. Measuring dollar volume relative to the coin's own past (20/60) and using a log level both came out flat (+0.0010 and +0.0011), and both had inconsistent signs across periods. The one form that works is the scale-free rank of dollar volume averaged over a few days: coins trading well below their own dollar-volume norm do better afterwards, with the negative sign as the idea requires.

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's range: closing near the high means buyers dominated the session. I'll measure it as a fraction — close divided by high, which is unit-free and comparable across coins — and average it over a short window so one noisy day doesn't dominate.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0476
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0210 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0277, 2023 +0.0195, 2024 +0.0191

That's already a strong start: incremental IC +0.0210 with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods. Since a single day's close-to-high fraction is noisy, I'll try smoothing the same quantity with a short EMA instead of a plain mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0482
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0195 (t = 8.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0255, 2023 +0.0172, 2024 +0.0188

The EMA version is weaker (+0.0195), so the plain short mean of the close-to-high fraction is better than any smoothing — I'll keep the mean form. Next I'll widen the averaging window to 10 days to see whether the effect needs more history before it shows up.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0505
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0158 (t = 7.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0180, 2023 +0.0136, 2024 +0.0169

The 10-day mean is clearly worse (+0.0158), so the effect is a short-lived one and the 5-day mean is the best so far. One more form worth checking: squaring the close-to-high fraction before averaging, which emphasizes days closing near the high and down-grades days closing near the low, keeping the same 5-day window.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0447
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0198 (t = -8.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0255, 2023 -0.0174, 2024 -0.0194

Squaring flips the sign to −0.0198 with t = −8.3, so the sign is entirely driven by the idea's direction: closing near the high *does* predict outperformance, but the squared form is mostly capturing the opposite-of-the-idea case (days closing near the low). That's two tests in a row that failed to beat the 5-day mean, so I'll stop and hand in the best-tested one.

What I found: measuring the close's position inside the day's range as close/high and averaging it over 5 days gives a rank IC of +0.048 and an incremental IC of +0.0210 (t = 8.7) with the same sign in all three sub-periods (+0.028, +0.020, +0.019), so the idea holds on this history and it is not just a repackaged liquidity or reversal effect. Shorter averaging (10 days) and more extreme weighting (squared) both weaken it, which says the signal is short-lived and it is the level of the close-to-high fraction that matters, not the extremes.

<factor>(Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high')) - 1).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about the daily high-low range: a wider range should mean a worse next-day return, so the factor is the negative of the range, and the range must be a ratio of prices so it is comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest form — the log of high/low, averaged over 5 days — to see how much of it survives after the known styles are removed.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The simplest form already gives +0.0203 incremental IC with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so the idea holds. Next I'll check whether the raw level of range is mostly a volatility proxy — I'll compress the range with a 20-day median instead of a mean, which is less sensitive to a few extreme days.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0521
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0108 (t = 4.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0122, 2023 +0.0066, 2024 +0.0142

The 20-day median is clearly weaker (+0.0108 vs +0.0203), so the level of range is not just a volatility proxy — the level form is the better carrier of the idea. Now I'll check whether a short, 5-day average of the range is more responsive to a coin's recent range than the 20-day one, since the idea is about a daily tendency.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190

The 5-day average gives the same +0.0203 as the 20-day one, so the horizon is not the differentiator — the level of range is the thing that matters, and it is the 20-day median that is worse. One more variant on the same idea: rank each day's range across coins and then average the ranks over 5 days, so the factor measures how consistently a coin's range sits at the top of the cross-section rather than its raw level.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0591
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0190 (t = 7.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0295, 2023 +0.0143, 2024 +0.0185
